identification.summary: Manatee Tempest (formerly DEV-0243) is a ransomware-associated activity group whose activity Microsoft says overlaps with what other vendors track as EvilCorp [S1][S2]. Microsoft cites Dridex as one of the earliest campaigns that made the group notorious [S2]. It has deployed the custom WastedLocker ransomware, the in-house PhoenixLocker and Macaw payloads, and, from around November 2021, the LockBit 2.0 RaaS payload [S1]. It buys access from the access broker DEV-0206 (Mustard Tempest), whose FakeUpdates/SocGholish infections hand off to Manatee Tempest hands-on-keyboard activity [S1][S2][S7]. Microsoft named it among ransomware operators using the ESXi 'ESX Admins' technique in 2024 [S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft gives no first-seen date. It cites Dridex as one of the group's earliest campaigns [S2] and first saw it deploying LockBit RaaS payloads in November 2021 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Manatee Tempest. 'DEV-0243 is now tracked as Manatee Tempest' per Microsoft's April 2023 update note [S2]. Microsoft's naming map lists origin Russia and other names DEV-0243 and INDRIK SPIDER [S5]. Microsoft also maps INDRIK SPIDER to Mustard Tempest (DEV-0206, financially motivated), the SocGholish access broker. Treat the two as separate Microsoft clusters that work in partnership, not one actor [S1][S5][S7]. MITRE tracks the ransomware/Dridex cluster as Indrik Spider (G0119) and the access broker as Mustard Tempest (G1020) [S6][S7].

attribution.sponsor: Financially motivated cybercriminal group. Microsoft lists its origin as Russia [S5]. The cited sources do not establish a state sponsor.
attribution.confidence: Microsoft says DEV-0243 'falls under activities tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp' [S1]. In separate reporting it says the group overlaps with EvilCorp activity [S2]. Microsoft assesses that the move to LockBit 2.0 is 'likely an attempt by DEV-0243 to avoid attribution to their group' [S1]. No government attribution statement was retrieved for this file.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and incident observations: custom Cobalt Strike loaders after DEV-0206 access [S1], Dridex-like code and behavior in Raspberry Robin/Fauppod samples, which Microsoft presents as supporting rather than conclusive evidence [S2], and ESXi intrusion observations [S3]. Microsoft notes the group's 'sanctioned status', which may discourage victims from paying, but does not name the sanctioning authority [S1].

objectives: Financial gain through ransomware extortion, preceded by Dridex-era banking-malware operations [S1][S2]. Microsoft assesses that the group switched to the LockBit 2.0 RaaS payload to avoid attribution, because its sanctioned status could discourage victims from paying [S1].

targeting.notes: The Microsoft sources gathered do not name sectors or regions for Manatee Tempest. Targets are enterprise networks reached through DEV-0206 FakeUpdates access or Raspberry Robin infections [S1][S2]. Known targets also include domain-joined VMware ESXi hypervisors [S3] and hybrid on-premises/cloud environments [S4]. Raspberry Robin, a delivery path to this cluster, had payload-related alerts on nearly 3,000 devices in almost 1,000 organizations over 30 days in 2022, but that figure covers Raspberry Robin overall, not Manatee Tempest victims [S2].

capabilities.summary: Hands-on-keyboard ransomware operator. It enters through access bought from the DEV-0206 FakeUpdates/SocGholish JavaScript framework and is linked to custom Cobalt Strike loaders [S1]. Its payloads are WastedLocker, PhoenixLocker and Macaw (in-house), and LockBit 2.0 RaaS from around November 2021 [S1]. FakeUpdates delivered through Raspberry Robin USB-worm infections from July 2022 led to follow-on activity resembling DEV-0243 pre-ransomware behavior [S1][S2]. Microsoft names Manatee Tempest among ransomware operators that create an 'ESX Admins' domain group to gain full administrative control of domain-joined ESXi hosts (CVE-2024-37085) for mass encryption of VMs [S3]. Microsoft has also observed it targeting both on-premises and cloud environments and exploiting the interfaces between them [S4]. MITRE lists Dridex, BitPaymer, WastedLocker, Cobalt Strike, Empire, Mimikatz, PsExec and Donut as associated software [S6].

campaigns.name: DEV-0206 partnership and WastedLocker ransomware
campaigns.summary: In its first partnerships with DEV-0206, the group deployed the custom WastedLocker ransomware after SocGholish access, then moved to the in-house PhoenixLocker and Macaw payloads.

campaigns.name: Adoption of LockBit 2.0 RaaS payload
campaigns.summary: Around November 2021 the group began deploying LockBit 2.0. Microsoft assesses this was likely an effort to avoid attribution tied to its sanctioned status.

campaigns.name: Raspberry Robin to FakeUpdates handoff
campaigns.summary: Microsoft saw FakeUpdates delivered through existing Raspberry Robin infections, followed by actions resembling DEV-0243 pre-ransomware behavior. Dridex-like traits in Fauppod add supporting evidence.

campaigns.name: Microsoft renames DEV-0243 to Manatee Tempest
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's taxonomy update renamed DEV-0243 to Manatee Tempest.

campaigns.name: ESXi 'ESX Admins' technique (CVE-2024-37085)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft names Manatee Tempest among ransomware operators using the ESX Admins group technique against domain-joined ESXi hypervisors in numerous attacks.

diamond.adversary: Manatee Tempest (DEV-0243), which overlaps with EvilCorp. Microsoft lists its origin as Russia, and it is a sanctioned group [S1][S2][S5].
diamond.capability: Custom Cobalt Strike loaders. WastedLocker, PhoenixLocker, Macaw and LockBit 2.0 ransomware. A Dridex lineage. ESX Admins group abuse (CVE-2024-37085) [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.infrastructure: Access bought from DEV-0206 FakeUpdates/SocGholish malvertising. Raspberry Robin USB-worm infections whose payloads sit on compromised QNAP NAS devices and Tor-hosted C2 [S1][S2]. Microsoft attributes those components to related clusters, not to Manatee Tempest itself.
diamond.victim: Enterprise networks with domain-joined ESXi hypervisors and hybrid on-premises/cloud estates. No sector or regional victimology appears in the sources gathered [S3][S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated ransomware extortion. Sanctioned status gives the group a reason to rebrand payloads and hide behind RaaS brands [S1].
diamond.technology: Windows Active Directory domains, VMware ESXi joined to AD, and hybrid identity links between on-premises and cloud [S3][S4].

gaps: Only microsoft.com was reachable in this session, and the web-search budget was used up. The CrowdStrike Indrik Spider report, Krebs 'Inside Evil Corp', BBC WastedLocker coverage, Secureworks GOLD DRAKE profile, Wikipedia (Maksim Yakubets) and MITRE G0119/G1020 pages in the record's references could not be opened. The imported summary claims (Dridex since June 2014, BitPaymer and the August 2017 NHS ransom) are therefore unverified here.

US government actions (the December 2019 DOJ indictment and Treasury/OFAC sanctions on Evil Corp members) and the 2024 UK/US/Australia follow-on actions were not retrieved. Microsoft refers only to the group's 'sanctioned status' without naming the authority [S1].
Reported Evil Corp links to Russian intelligence services are not covered in any source gathered. Do not assert state direction from this file.

Cluster boundary: Microsoft maps INDRIK SPIDER to both Manatee Tempest and Mustard Tempest [S5]. MITRE's Indrik Spider (G0119) may cover activity Microsoft splits between the two. Mandiant UNC2165 and Secureworks GOLD DRAKE aliases in the record were not confirmed against their vendor sources.
No sector or geographic victimology for Manatee Tempest is published in the Microsoft sources gathered.
Which ransomware Manatee Tempest deployed in the 2024 ESXi intrusions is not stated. Microsoft ties Akira and Black Basta to other operators in that report [S3].
Post-2024 Manatee Tempest activity was not found in Microsoft blog search results reviewed on 2026-10-14.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key terrain is Active Directory, domain-joined ESXi hypervisors hosting mission VMs, and hybrid identity links between on-premises and cloud [S3][S4]. Removable media and user web browsing are entry points, through Raspberry Robin USB infections and FakeUpdates fake browser-update lures [S1][S2]. STEP 2 (effects): A single domain group created at the hypervisor layer can let an attacker encrypt many VMs at once, which turns one compromised account into a base-wide outage [S3]. STEP 3 (adversary template): access purchased from DEV-0206 (SocGholish JavaScript) or Raspberry Robin, then a Cobalt Strike loader, then credential and AD abuse, then ESX Admins group creation, then ransomware such as WastedLocker or LockBit, often under a borrowed RaaS brand [S1][S2][S3]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic ransomware against any organization whose access is sold to the group, including DoD-adjacent contractors. MDCOA is hypervisor-level mass encryption that disables mission systems hosted on virtualized infrastructure [S3]. Candidate indicators: creation of or changes to an 'ESX Admins' AD group, FakeUpdates JavaScript execution from browser-update lures, msiexec launched from LNK files on USB drives that reaches external NAS hosts, and Tor C2 traffic [S2][S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: feed ESXi patch state for CVE-2024-37085 and alerts on 'ESX Admins' group changes into the common operating picture, and treat hypervisors as critical assets [S3]. (2) Authorities: the group is sanctioned and uses other RaaS brands to avoid attribution, so ransom-note branding alone cannot determine the actor; coordinate legal and payment questions through proper channels [S1]. (3) Mission assurance: back up and segment the virtualization management plane, and plan continuity for mass loss of VMs [S3]. (4) Coordination: access often comes from a separate broker cluster (Mustard Tempest/DEV-0206). Share indicators across the access-broker and ransomware stages with DC3, DIB partners and cloud tenants, because the actor exploits on-premises-to-cloud interfaces [S1][S4].
